extracted.intended_audience: EPA writers, communications staff, and others producing EPA public communications (press releases, fact sheets, web content, reports)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for writing and producing EPA public communications (press releases, web pages, fact sheets, reports), including grammar, punctuation, structure, tone, procedural steps, and values such as accuracy and inclusiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core style standard — Associated Press (AP)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA writing style is, at its core, the AP Stylebook; in the great majority of cases regarding grammar and usage, EPA follows AP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA has an intranet subscription to AP. Use AP as primary reference for grammar, punctuation, and usage. EPA supplements or modifies AP in specific instances noted in this stylebook. AP updates conventions periodically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations and acronyms
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out abbreviations and acronyms the first time they appear on a page; abbreviations are acceptable thereafter and may be used with or without a definite article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always spell out 'United States' when it appears as a noun. 'Southwest' is one word; abbreviated 'SW'. As an adjective, 'U.S.' is acceptable. State abbreviations: use non-Postal abbreviations (Ala., Ariz., etc.) with city names; eight states are not abbreviated in text (Alaska, Hawaii, Idaho, Iowa, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Utah). Use two-letter Postal Service abbreviations only with full addresses and ZIP codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ampersand usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ampersands (&) only when they are part of a formal name or when space is at a premium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: C & O Railroad; otherwise write 'and'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bylines and staff credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Bylines (credits) in government publications are confined to authors of articles and photographers who originated pictures; author is someone who conceived or is responsible for the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not extend 'author' to supervisors, advisors, or committee members—list them under 'acknowledgments' instead. Acknowledgements allowed (not thanks/dedications). Contractor staff names should not be listed; contractor firm names discouraged unless necessary. Contract numbers may be listed. EPA is responsible for contractor work once published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize only where appropriate: titles and lists capitalize first word and proper nouns; many common terms and chemical names are lowercase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize terms such as 'waste management, disposal, pollution prevention, non-governmental organization, legislation, project, offices, endnote, sector' or chemical names like 'lead, mercury, dioxins.' Capitalize 'Agency' when referring specifically to EPA. Lowercase 'federal, local, native, state, tribal' unless part of an official title. 'Internet' is a proper noun; capitalize. Capitalize 'Region' when referring to a specific EPA regional office; otherwise lowercase geographic regions. 'Section, article' are not capitalized. Use 'Title' capitalized when referring to a part of law/regulation. Follow AP guidance on 'web' and related words (webpage, webmaster, webcast one word, lowercase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific disclaimers when documents include non-EPA authors, drafts, or commercial references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-EPA authors: include statement that views are authors' own and not necessarily EPA's. Draft documents: mark as draft and advise not to quote or cite. Commercial references: include disclaimer that mention does not convey EPA approval or endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider diversity in the development of every communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure materials reflect a diversity of perspectives and are fair and accurate; emphasize diversity and encourage learners/readers to explore different perspectives when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender-neutral language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid gender bias; use gender-neutral words and constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult resources such as the U.S. Department of Labor's Dictionary of Occupational Titles or The Nonsexist Word Finder. Use plural constructions or reword to avoid awkward 'he or she' formulations when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers — AP conventions and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out whole numbers below 10; use figures for 10 and above, with common exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions include ages (a 5-year-old), percentages (3 percent), monetary amounts (6 cents), and numbers at the beginning of a sentence (spell out). Follow AP for more exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use active voice as much as possible because it is stronger, clearer, and more actionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passive voice can obscure actors (e.g., 'mistakes were made'); prefer 'EPA will issue a proposed cleanup plan this summer' rather than 'A cleanup plan will be issued this summer.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain language requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use plain language so audiences can understand communications the first time they read or hear them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain language is defined by results—easy to read, understand, and use. Additional guidance available from plainlanguage.gov. Use structural elements (lead, clear organization) to support plain language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional designations clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume readers know regional numbers; explicitly list states or use named regional descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Region 5 (IL, IN, MI, MN, OH, WI)' or use 'EPA New England.' Use 'EPA regional offices' instead of 'EPA regions.' Use Arabic numerals for Regions (Region 5, not Region V).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling: one word vs two vs hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow AP conventions on compound words commonly in question (cleanup, email, groundwater, listserv, online, stormwater, water body, webpage vs home page).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: noun/adjective 'cleanup' vs verb 'clean up'; 'email' preferred over 'e-mail'; 'groundwater' one word; 'listserv' not 'listserve'; 'webpage' one word (but 'home page' two words). Avoid hyphenated forms unless required to prevent ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles: restrict to two levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep titles to one main title and, if needed, one subtitle; the subtitle is separated by a colon in references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For clarity and bibliographic needs, place a key word at the beginning of the title when possible; use generic phrases in subtitles (e.g., 'Report to Congress') rather than in main title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common words & structure pitfalls (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid common usage errors and know correct meanings for often-confused words and constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides guidance and examples on: affect/effect; bad/badly; capitalization of 'bay' after a proper name; contractions and pronoun/verb confusions; compose/comprise; dispose vs dispose of; good/well; figuratively/literally/virtually; overuse of 'impact' as a verb (prefer 'affect'); misuse of 'may' (means permission, not possibility); 'migrate' transitive vs intransitive; use of 'that' vs 'this' and 'that' vs 'which'; 'waste' as inherently plural. Use these examples to choose correct words and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing for children and educators
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow NAAEE guidelines when preparing environmental education materials for kids, students, and educators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: fairness and accuracy; appropriate depth for developmental levels; emphasis on skills building (critical thinking/problem solving); action orientation promoting civic responsibility; instructional soundness (multiple learning methods and connect to everyday experiences); usability (well designed, adaptable, accompanied by instructor support). Consult Environmental Education Materials: Guidelines for Excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation: apostrophes and possessives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use apostrophes for possessives and avoid using apostrophes to form plurals of abbreviations and acronyms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'PCBs' for plural; 'EPA's policy' for possessive. Follow AP for other apostrophe rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serial (Oxford) comma guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: AP generally recommends against the serial comma but allows exceptions when clarity requires it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not put a comma before the conjunction in a simple series ('red, white and blue'). Put a comma before the final conjunction if an integral element requires a conjunction or in complex series of phrases where items include commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exclamation marks sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid exclamation points except in rare, appropriate contexts; rely on words and ideas to convey enthusiasm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive use undermines tone (e.g., comic-book style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation to prevent ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hyphens when two words together form a single adjective before a noun; omit hyphens when adjectives follow nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'free-form sculpture' (before noun) vs 'The sculpture was free form' (after noun). If hyphens are disliked, rewrite the sentence to avoid them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods and sentence spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use one space after periods, not two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP dictates one space after closing periods (except with initials like C.S. Lewis) because desktop publishing adjusts spacing automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation mark punctuation and dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for short quotes and dialogue; follow standard punctuation placement rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each speaker's words get a separate paragraph. Periods and commas go inside quotation marks; dashes, semicolons, question marks, and exclamation points go inside when they apply to the quoted material, outside when they apply to the whole sentence. Use single quotes for quotations within quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use semicolons to join related independent clauses, before conjunctive adverbs/transitions, or to separate complex list elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: join two independent clauses where the second restates the first; use before conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore, etc.); use to separate items in a series when items themselves include commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bulleted and vertical list punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate punctuation and capitalization in lists; AP uses dashes in news stories after a colon, and EPA follows AP conventions; for complex vertical lists follow Chicago Manual rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After a colon, items that are complete sentences should be capitalized and end with periods. For vertical lists that complete a sentence and include internal punctuation, semicolons may be used between items and a period after the final item; begin each item with lowercase unless they are complete sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar: agreement and common errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure pronoun-antecedent and subject-verb agreement; avoid unclear collective subject constructions and incorrect pronoun forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'If one is nervous, he should relax' (not 'they'); make subjects plural when possible to avoid awkward 'he or she' constructions. Learn use of I vs me (subject vs object), and ensure verbs agree with chosen subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunction and preposition placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional grammar disfavors starting sentences with conjunctions and ending sentences with prepositions but EPA accepts exceptions where effective communication benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conjunctions to connect ideas within sentences, but beginning a sentence with a conjunction may be effective. Ending with prepositions is common and sometimes acceptable in colloquial tone, but reword if strict formal English is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptical/incomplete sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Elliptical sentences (missing subject/predicate) are grammatically incorrect but can be effective and acceptable in the right context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use them sparingly and only when context makes meaning clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split infinitives
rubrics_metrics.description: Split infinitives are not forbidden but should be used sparingly; they are 'seldom-seldom' in EPA style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If splitting an infinitive gives proper emphasis or clarity, it can be acceptable; otherwise prefer alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and structure as paramount
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity is the most important quality in EPA writing; structure and style should serve clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key elements of structure include consistency, coherence, direction, integration, and plain language. Use parallel construction, consistent spelling/punctuation, and maintain voice and person. Headlines should reflect topic and draw readers in. Vary sentence length but aim for short, tight sentences; if long sentences are necessary, sandwich them between short ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of interest (lead-first structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure communications to begin with the lead/key selling point/main theme—the idea of greatest interest to the audience—then expand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell readers up front why the material benefits them and what you want them to learn or do. Use subheadings for scannability. Summarize at the end when appropriate to lead to a decision or action. Alternative structures (chronological, dramatic, logical) are sometimes useful but often less effective for busy audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: affirmation, person, voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Match tone to content; prefer positive statements, active voice, and second person where appropriate to be friendly and interactive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use positive commands (e.g., 'Leave the valve open' vs 'Do not close the valve') for clarity. Press releases and technical documents are usually third person. Use second person for actionable guidance. Tone must be appropriate and consistent with intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid borrowed style and mimicry
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not copy popular advertising or other organizations' distinctive styles just because they are popular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowed approaches may not be creative for your organization and may not work for different audiences. If an approach genuinely generates desired actions, it may be used, but don't mimic solely for trendiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichés, jargon, and 'hip' language
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use clichés, jargon, or trendy 'hip' language in general-purpose communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions allowed if the usage is intentionally humorous and effective. Jargon isolates readers and reduces clarity; prefer plain language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition vs redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate repetition (useful in teaching and marketing) from redundancy (unnecessary repetition); avoid redundancy but use repetition deliberately when instructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In journalism most repetition is redundant; in education/marketing purposeful repetition reinforces messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: No self-aggrandizement; public-interest communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications must not serve to promote the agency, officials, or budgets; they must serve the public interest and avoid self-congratulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal statute prohibits using appropriated funds for agency self-interest. Avoid congratulatory acknowledgements. It is appropriate to identify responsible offices or contacts. Reports should be honest and include mistakes/failures where relevant; success stories should reflect EPA's role appropriately (helped, not did). Contractors may be cited by firm/contract number but individual contractor staff names should not be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep communications simple but sufficiently deep
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity does not mean meager content; tailor depth to the audience and do not condescend to learners who may want detailed information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know your audience and provide enough information for interested citizens to become informed; be clear but not patronizing. Offer pathways for deeper engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of subjunctive/hedging responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid unqualified subjunctive or speculative statements that are not actionable or that may scare; provide circumstances or probabilities when making risk statements or enforcement possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not say 'This chemical can cause cancer' without context about conditions or probability. If you say 'EPA might enforce these regulations' clarify under what circumstances and likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process: planning, review, and editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow a process of brainstorming, outlining, involving reviewers early, and rigorous editing/proofreading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brainstorm and outline main message and audience. Involve product review officers and program reviewers from concept stage. Include main message in paragraph one (lead). Spell-check and proofread for common confusable words. Ask at least one other person to edit. Use Flesch-Kincaid readability statistics in Word to check grade level. Use AP Stylebook as primary reference and Webster's as official spelling guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy, honesty, and openness as core substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Honesty and factual accuracy are the basis of all EPA communications; verify facts and coordinate to avoid contradictions across the Agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow a 'courtroom' standard: truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Verification involves checking accuracy during writing and verifying to the audience via citations, explanations of basis, and clear sourcing. Use product review processes to coordinate across offices and prevent apparent contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias for action and public involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications should, where appropriate, drive action and involve the public at levels desired and needed by EPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most EPA communications should enable action—give clear steps, resources, or reasons for involvement. Simply informing is sometimes enough, but default to making information usable and actionable whenever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusiveness in audience reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure communications are understandable and usable by everyone in the scope of EPA's work; target specific audiences but aim to include the broad public as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate so that 'everybody understands' and can use the information. Avoid excluding groups through jargon, tone, or inaccessible formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference resources to use
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specified authoritative references for style and spelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary style reference: Associated Press Stylebook. Official spelling guide: Webster's (Merriam-Webster's Collegiate Dictionary). Use these references when questions arise.
